content: An F-test is a type of statistical test where the test statistic follows an F-distribution under the assumption that the null hypothesis is true. The term F-test was introduced by George W. Snedecor in recognition of Sir Ronald A. Fisher, who originally developed the statistic as a variance ratio in the 1920s. One common application of the F-test is to evaluate the hypothesis that the means of multiple normally distributed populations, all with the same standard deviation, are equal. This is the most widely recognized use of the F-test and represents the simplest scenario in the analysis of variance (ANOVA). Another application of the F-test is to test the hypothesis that the standard deviations of two normally distributed populations are equal, implying that the populations are of comparable origin. However, it is important to note that the F-test is highly sensitive to deviations from normality. Even minor departures from a normal distribution can render the test unreliable, making it unsuitable for such data. The F-test statistic can often be calculated through a straightforward procedure. This involves comparing two regression models: one that imposes constraints on one or more regression coefficients as specified by the null hypothesis, and another that does not impose these constraints. The test statistic is derived from a modified ratio of the residual sum of squares (RSS) of the two models. To calculate the F statistic, consider two models, referred to as model 1 and model 2. Model 1 is nested within model 2, meaning that model 1 has fewer parameters (p1) than model 2 (p2), where p2 > p1. For example, a simple linear regression model ( y = mx + b ) has two parameters (p = 2). If there are n data points available to estimate the parameters of both models, the F statistic is calculated as follows: [ F = frac{(RSS_1 RSS_2) / (p2 p1)}{RSS_2 / (n p2)} ] Here, ( RSS_i ) represents the residual sum of squares for model ( i ). If the regression model incorporates weights, ( RSS_i ) is replaced by ( chi^2 ), the weighted sum of squared residuals. The F statistic follows an F-distribution with degrees of freedom ( (p2 p1, n p2) ). The probability that the reduction in ( chi^2 ) associated with adding ( p2 p1 ) parameters is due to random chance is determined by the F-distribution at the calculated value. The null hypothesis, which states that none of the additional ( p2 p1 ) parameters are significantly correlated with the model, is rejected if the calculated F exceeds the critical value of F for a chosen significance level (e.g., ( p = 0.05 )). Tables of critical F values are widely available in statistical textbooks and resources.
